summary: On 20 September 2015 a brief network disruption made DynamoDB storage servers time out on membership requests. Their retries overloaded the metadata service and DynamoDB error rates reached about 55 percent for hours.

overview.background: DynamoDB storage servers hold table partitions and regularly ask a metadata service for their membership, meaning which partitions they serve. Many AWS services use DynamoDB for their own data.
overview.impact: DynamoDB error rates reached about 55 percent from 2:37 AM PDT, a level AWS said was higher than any seen in the previous three years. SQS, Auto Scaling, CloudWatch and console logins were also affected.
overview.severity: A region-wide event in US-East. AWS gives no formal severity number.
overview.gaps: The page does not state the year, and gives no logs.

diagrams.caption: After a brief network disruption, some metadata replies took longer than storage servers allowed. Those servers removed themselves, and their retries slowed the metadata service for everyone.

timeline.e: A brief network disruption affects some DynamoDB storage servers.
CloudWatch begins showing delayed and missing EC2 metrics.
DynamoDB customer error rates reach about 55 percent.
The team pauses requests to the metadata service to reduce the retry load.
DynamoDB finishes disabling traffic and the console shows login latency.
Error rates are low enough for most customers and dependent services.
EC2 Auto Scaling clears its backlog.
A residual 0.15 to 0.25 percent error rate is traced to one metadata partition and fixed.

rootCause.trigger: A brief network disruption slowed metadata responses past the timeout storage servers allowed.
rootCause.underlying: Rapid adoption of Global Secondary Indexes had grown the membership lists, making metadata replies slower, and the service lacked capacity and monitoring for that growth. Retries from unavailable servers made healthy servers fail renewals too.
contributing: No monitoring of membership list size
Retries added load during the failure

evidence.label: The decision
evidence.body: we decided to pause requests to the metadata service

evidence.label: The principle
evidence.body: For us, availability is the most important feature of DynamoDB

evidence.label: A simulated timeout setting
evidence.body:
membership_refresh:
  timeout_ms: 2000
  retry:
    backoff: exponential
    jitter: full
    max_inflight_per_node: 1
evidence.note: Shows limits that stop a fleet flooding a metadata service. Invented.

diagnose.step: Look at the metadata service latency and the size of its replies.
diagnose.why: Slow replies explain why healthy servers drop out.
A rising count shows a spiral.

diagnose.step: Check what retries the failed servers are sending.
diagnose.why: Retry load can exceed normal load.

correct.step: Pause or throttle requests to the metadata service.
correct.why: AWS paused them to let it recover.

verify.step: Watch error rates and dependent services separately.
verify.why: Auto Scaling and CloudWatch recovered later.

verify.step: Look for residual partitions with low traffic.
verify.why: A hidden partition caused the small residual errors.

prevent.step: Alert on growth of membership lists.
Rate limit refresh requests and lengthen query time limits.
Split the metadata service into parts.

fix.safety: Pausing requests deliberately makes the outage worse for a while. Do it only when retries are the cause and you can bring traffic back in steps.

troubleshoot.scenario: Storage nodes keep dropping out after a short network blip. The membership service is slow and busier than usual.
clues: Every dropped node retries at once
troubleshoot.question: What do you do?
troubleshoot.answer: Pause or throttle membership requests so the metadata service recovers, add capacity, and bring nodes back in stages. Then add monitoring for list size and rate limits.

rootcause.q: Why did healthy servers start to fail?
options: Retries from unavailable servers loaded the metadata service
rootcause.why: AWS says retries added load and caused renewals to fail.

remediation.answer: Alert when membership list size or metadata p99 latency exceeds a threshold well below the storage-server timeout.
Exponential back-off with jitter and a cap on concurrent refreshes.
Partition storage servers by range, with a metadata instance per partition group.

design.prompt: Design a metadata path that stays healthy when its clients all retry.
design.answer: Shard the metadata service, rate limit clients, cache membership, back off with jitter and monitor sizes and latencies.

checks.q: What error rate did DynamoDB reach?

checks.why: AWS says rapid adoption increased membership list sizes.

checks.q: Which service had a backlog until 10:52 AM?
checks.why: AWS says Auto Scaling cleared its backlog then.

options: To cut retry load so it could recover

recovery: Pause retries to let the core recover
practices: Treat dependent services as part of the blast radius
